Laxatives are used to treat
constipation
if lifestyle changes haven’t helped.
Laxatives are available over-the-counter, without a prescription. You can also get them from pharmacies and supermarkets.
Types of laxatives
There are many different types of laxatives, including:
bulk-forming laxatives – increase the bulk of your poo to make it easier to pass
osmotic laxatives – soften your poo to make it easier to pass
stimulant laxatives – speed up the movement of your bowels
stool softener laxatives – increase the fluid content of poo to make it easier to pass
Laxatives are available as:
tablets
capsules
sachets of powder you mix with water and then drink
suppositories – a capsule you place inside your back passage (rectum) that dissolves
liquids or gels that you place directly into your back passage
How to take laxatives
Most adults should try using a bulk-forming laxative first. Bulk-forming laxatives usually start to work after about 2 or 3 days.
If your poo remains hard, try using an osmotic laxative with, or instead of, a bulk-forming laxative. Osmotic laxatives usually start to work after about 2 or 3 days.
If your poo is soft, but is still difficult to pass, try taking a stimulant laxative with a bulk-forming laxative. Stimulant laxatives usually have an effect within 6 to 12 hours.
Do
only use laxatives occasionally
only use laxatives for short periods of time
stop taking laxatives once your condition improves
read the patient information leaflet that comes with your medication so you know how to take it properly
ask your pharmacist for further advice if you’re not sure how to take your medication
follow the advice of your healthcare professional if you’re taking laxatives for a longer period
drink lots of water while taking bulk-forming or osmotic laxatives
Don’t
do not get into the habit of taking laxatives every day to ease your constipation – this can be harmful
do not take more than the recommended dose of laxatives
Possible side effects
Laxatives can cause side effects. These are usually mild and should pass once you stop taking the medication.
Speak to your GP practice if you experience worrying or persistent side effects while taking laxatives.
Common side effects
Common side effects of laxatives include:
bloating
farting
painful stomach cramps
feeling sick
dehydration
Less common side effects
Using laxatives too much, or for a long period of time, can also cause:
diarrhoea
intestinal obstruction (where the bowel becomes blocked by large, dry stools)
unbalanced levels of salts and minerals in your body
Speak to your pharmacist or GP practice if:
you’re unsure what laxative to use
you’re still constipated after trying different types of laxative
you think your child might need laxatives
your constipation hasn’t improved after taking laxatives for more than a week
lifestyle changes and laxatives haven’t helped your constipation
Warnings and precautions
Check with your pharmacist or GP practice before using laxatives if you have:
a bowel condition, like
irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
or
Crohn’s disease
a
colostomy
or
ileostomy
a history of liver or kidney disease
an obstruction somewhere in your digestive system
diabetes
difficulties swallowing (dysphagia)
a
lactose intolerance
phenylketonuria (a rare genetic condition)
Children
Laxatives aren’t usually recommended for children, unless advised by a doctor. Always check with your GP practice before giving your baby or child a laxative.
Laxatives aren’t recommended for babies who haven’t been weaned. If your baby is constipated, try giving them extra water between feeds. Gently massaging their tummy and moving their legs in a cycling motion may also help. Babies who are eating solid foods may be able to use laxatives. But you should make sure your baby drinks plenty of water or diluted fruit juice first. You should also increase the amount of
fibre
in their diet.
In older children, osmotic or stimulant laxatives may be recommended. This is alongside dietary changes.
Other medicines and laxatives
Before using laxatives, read the patient information leaflet that comes with the medication. This will let you know if it’s safe for you to take.
Check with your GP practice or pharmacist before using laxatives if you are taking opioid painkillers. For example, codeine or morphine.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
You should check before taking laxatives if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding. You may be able to use laxatives but certain types of laxative may be more suitable for you than others.
Alternatives to taking laxatives
It’s often possible to improve constipation without having to use laxatives.
Before trying laxatives, it may help to make some lifestyle changes. You can:
eat more
fibre
drink plenty of water
exercise regularly
